# `linear_generic_param`: a linear value is passed to a generic parameter that has not opted in

A linear value is passed to a function that is generic in that parameter
(`fn pass(x) do x end`). An ordinary type variable is unrestricted, so the
function body could copy or drop the value, and the compiler does not look
inside the body to find out.

## A program that triggers it

```march
mod Main do
  needs IO.Console
  always_linear type Token = Token(Int)

  fn consume(t : Token) : Int do
    match t do Token(n) -> n end
  end

  fn pass(x) do x end

  fn main(_console : Cap(IO.Console)) do
    let t = pass(Token(1))
    println(int_to_string(consume(t)))
  end
end
```

## The fix

If the generic function uses the parameter exactly once, mark it `linear`
where the function is defined (`linear x : a`). That opts it in to
receiving linear values, and its body is then checked to use `x` once.
Otherwise, consume the value at the call site instead.

```march
mod Main do
  needs IO.Console
  always_linear type Token = Token(Int)

  fn consume(t : Token) : Int do
    match t do Token(n) -> n end
  end

  fn pass(linear x : a) : a do x end

  fn main(_console : Cap(IO.Console)) do
    let t = pass(Token(1))
    println(int_to_string(consume(t)))
  end
end
```

## Why the rule exists

A type variable used to be unrestricted *and* instantiable with a linear
type, so `fn dup(x) do (x, x) end` turned one linear value into two.
Requiring the opt-in keeps generic code usable with ordinary values and
makes the functions that may receive linear values say so.

See also: [the language reference](../linear-types.md).
